# `silk/crypto/x25519`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

Agree on a shared secret with X25519 (RFC 7748) Diffie-Hellman.

## When to use
Use [`X25519`](#X25519) when two parties must get the same secret over a channel that others can read,
for example in a TLS 1.3 or Noise handshake. Each side makes a key with [`X25519.generate`](#X25519.impl.generate),
sends [`X25519.publicKey`](#X25519.impl.publicKey), and calls [`X25519.agree`](#X25519.impl.agree) with the public key of the other side.
Then derive the real keys from the shared secret with `silk.crypto.hkdf`.

## Details
Secrets, public keys, and shared secrets are 32 bytes, little-endian. A secret is clamped as RFC
7748 says, so all 32-byte values are valid. [`X25519.agree`](#X25519.impl.agree) consumes the key, because an
ephemeral key is for one exchange. Nothing allocates.

## Errors
- [`X25519Error`](#X25519Error) for an input with the wrong length, or for a peer key that gives an all-zero
  secret.

## Gotchas
The exchange does not tell you who the other side is. An attacker in the middle can run one
exchange with each side. Authenticate the exchange, for example with a certificate signature. Do
not use the shared secret directly as a key. The key is not erased when it is dropped.

## Examples
### Agree on a secret (RFC 7748 test vector)
```silk
import silk.core.result { Result }
import silk.crypto.x25519 { X25519, X25519Error }

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  // Real programs use `X25519.generate()` with a secure `Random` provider.
  let alice = match X25519.fromSecret(
    b"\x77\x07\x6d\x0a\x73\x18\xa5\x7d\x3c\x16\xc1\x72\x51\xb2\x66\x45\xdf\x4c\x2f\x87\xeb\xc0\x99\x2a\xb1\x77\xfb\xa5\x1d\xb9\x2c\x2a"
  ) {
    Result<X25519, X25519Error>.Success { value } => move value
    Result<X25519, X25519Error>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let bob = match X25519.fromSecret(
    b"\x5d\xab\x08\x7e\x62\x4a\x8a\x4b\x79\xe1\x7f\x8b\x83\x80\x0e\xe6\x6f\x3b\xb1\x29\x26\x18\xb6\xfd\x1c\x2f\x8b\x27\xff\x88\xe0\xeb"
  ) {
    Result<X25519, X25519Error>.Success { value } => move value
    Result<X25519, X25519Error>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let alicePublic = X25519.publicKey(&alice)
  let bobPublic = X25519.publicKey(&bob)
  let fromAlice = match X25519.agree(move alice, &bobPublic) {
    Result<[u8; 32], X25519Error>.Success { value } => value
    Result<[u8; 32], X25519Error>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }
  let fromBob = match X25519.agree(move bob, &alicePublic) {
    Result<[u8; 32], X25519Error>.Success { value } => value
    Result<[u8; 32], X25519Error>.Failure { error: _ } => {
      return 1
    }
  }

  // Both sides get 4a5d9d5b...1742.
  if alicePublic[0] != 0x85 || fromAlice[0] != 0x4a || fromBob[0] != 0x4a || fromBob[31] != 0x42 {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `X25519` with `import silk.crypto.x25519 { X25519 }`.

<a id="X25519Error.AllZeroSharedSecret"></a>

### `AllZeroSharedSecret`

```silk
AllZeroSharedSecret
```

The public key of the peer gives an all-zero shared secret. This occurs for a few low-order
points that a hostile peer can send.

<a id="X25519"></a>

## `X25519`

```silk
pub struct X25519
```

An X25519 key pair for one exchange: a secret and its public key.

### When to use
Use it when two parties must get the same secret over a channel that others can read, for
example in a TLS 1.3 or Noise handshake. Each side makes a key with [`X25519.generate`](#X25519.impl.generate), sends
[`X25519.publicKey`](#X25519.impl.publicKey), and calls [`X25519.agree`](#X25519.impl.agree) with the public key of the other side.

### Details
[`X25519.agree`](#X25519.impl.agree) consumes it. Make a new one for each exchange. Secrets, public keys, and shared
secrets are 32 bytes, little-endian. Nothing allocates.

### Gotchas
The exchange does not tell you who the other side is. An attacker in the middle can run one
exchange with each side. Authenticate the exchange, for example with a certificate signature.
Derive the real keys from the shared secret with `silk.crypto.hkdf`. The key is not erased when it is
dropped.

<a id="X25519.impl.fromSecret"></a>

### Associated function `fromSecret`

```silk
pub fn fromSecret(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<X25519, X25519Error>
```

Returns the key pair for the 32-byte secret `bytes`, after RFC 7748 clamping.

Use it for test vectors or a secret that you stored. The bytes are copied.

#### Errors
- `InvalidScalarLength` if `bytes` is not 32 bytes.

#### Gotchas
For a new exchange, use [`X25519.generate`](#X25519.impl.generate). A secret that is used for two exchanges gives the
same public key to both, so the exchanges can be linked.

<a id="X25519.impl.generate"></a>

### Associated function `generate`

```silk
pub effect fn generate() -> X25519 ? &mut Random
```

Returns a new key pair with a secret from 32 bytes of the ambient `Random`.

The `Random` provider must be cryptographically secure. If it fails, the program stops. There
is no fallback to a weaker source.

<a id="X25519.impl.publicKey"></a>

### Method `publicKey`

```silk
pub fn publicKey(self: &X25519) -> [u8; 32]
```

Returns the 32-byte public key to send to the peer. It does not consume the key pair.

<a id="X25519.impl.agree"></a>

### Method `agree`

```silk
pub fn agree(self: X25519, peer: &[u8]) -> Result<[u8; 32], X25519Error>
```

Returns the 32-byte shared secret for the public key `peer` of the other side, and consumes
the key pair.

As RFC 7748 says, the top bit of `peer` is ignored and any 32-byte value is accepted, also a
point that is not on the curve.

#### Errors
- `InvalidPeerLength` if `peer` is not 32 bytes.
- `AllZeroSharedSecret` if the result is all zeros. Stop the exchange.

The key pair is consumed also when it fails.

#### Gotchas
Pass the result through a key derivation function such as `silk.crypto.hkdf` before you use it as a
key.
